svg.title: API authorization, token verification, and consumption limits
svg.desc: Three panels. Broken object level authorization: swapping a resource identifier returns another user's object because the handler checked authentication but not ownership, remediated by an ownership check on every handler. JWT verification: rejecting the none algorithm, pinning the expected algorithm against RS256 to HS256 confusion, treating kid as untrusted, and validating issuer, audience and expiry. GraphQL and resource limits: introspection disabled in production, depth and cost ceilings, and rate limits applied per client identity rather than per IP alone.
svg.text: What an API has to check on every request
Four of the ten OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) entries are authorization failures. That concentration is the point of the list.
API1:2023 — BROKEN OBJECT LEVEL AUTHORIZATION
Authenticated is not authorized
A valid token for account 101 requests account 102, and the handler
returns it because it never compared the object owner to the subject.
Control
Load the object, compare its owner against the authenticated subject
through one shared authorization function, and return 404 rather than
403 wherever the existence of the object is itself sensitive.
JWT VERIFICATION — RFC 8725 / BCP 225
Never let the token decide how it is checked
Reject alg none. Pin the expected algorithm at the verifier, so a
rewrite from RS256 to HS256 cannot be signed with the public key.
Match kid against a known set; ignore or allowlist jku and x5u.
The more common production failure
Missing claim validation. Check iss, aud, and exp on every request —
without aud, a token minted for another service is accepted here.
QUERY COST AND RESOURCE CONSUMPTION — API4:2023
GraphQL hands query composition to the caller, so the server no longer controls the work per request
Disable introspection in production; cap query depth, per-field cost, alias repetition, and array batching.
Authorize inside resolvers — every resolver returning an object is its own object-level decision.
Rate-limit per client identity as well as per IP, and cap payload size, page size, timeouts, and metered downstream spend.
Between services, mutual TLS proves which workload is calling and nothing about whether it may act for this user — carry end-user context in a validated token.
Unguessable identifiers are hardening, never the authorization check: identifiers leak through logs, referrers, exports, and share links.
